questions.question:
A real (4x4) matrix A satisfies the equation [latex]A_{2} = I[/latex], where I is the (4x4)
identity matrix. The positive eigen value of A is _____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{since, }A^{2}=l, \text{eig}\left(A^{2}\right)&=\text{eig}(I)=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \text{eig}(A)^{2}&=1\\ \Rightarrow \quad \text{eig}(A)&=\pm 1 \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, the positive eigen value of A is +1.
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{since, }A^{2}=l, \text{eig}\left(A^{2}\right)&=\text{eig}(I)=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \text{eig}(A)^{2}&=1\\ \Rightarrow \quad \text{eig}(A)&=\pm 1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, the positive eigen value of A is +1.

questions.question:
The volume under the surface z(x,y) = x + y and above the triangle in the x-y
plane defined by [latex]\{0\leq y\leq x \; and \; 0\leq x\leq 12\}[/latex] is _____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Volume } &=\iint_{12 x} z d x d y=\iint(x+y) d x d y \\ &=\int_{0}^{12}\int_{0}^{x} \int(x+y) d x d y \\ &=\left.\int_{0}^{12}\left(x y+\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right) \right|_{0} ^{x} d x \\ &=\int_{0}^{12}\left(x^{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right) d x \\ &=\frac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{12} x^{2} d x=\frac{3}{2} \times\left.\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right|_{0} ^{12} \\ &=864 \text { unit }^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Volume } &=\iint_{12 x} z d x d y=\iint(x+y) d x d y \\ &=\int_{0}^{12}\int_{0}^{x} \int(x+y) d x d y \\ &=\left.\int_{0}^{12}\left(x y+\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right) \right|_{0} ^{x} d x \\ &=\int_{0}^{12}\left(x^{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right) d x \\ &=\frac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{12} x^{2} d x=\frac{3}{2} \times\left.\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right|_{0} ^{12} \\ &=864 \text { unit }^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

An unbiased coin is tossed an infinite number of times. The probability that the
fourth head appears at the tenth toss is
questions.explanation: It means 3-head appears in [latex]1^{\text {st }}[/latex] 9 trials. Probability of getting exactly 3 head in 1^{\text {st }} 9 trials [latex] \begin{aligned} &=\text{ Coefficient } p^{3}\text{ in }(4+p) 9 \\ \text{When, }&[\overline{p+q=1}] \\ &={ }^{9} C_{3} q^{6} p^{3}\\ \text{when, }\quad \rho&= \text{ probability of occure of head}\\ q &=\text { probability of occure of tail } \\ &={ }^{9} C_{3} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{6}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} \\ &={ }^{9} C_{3} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{9} \end{aligned}[/latex] and in [latex]10^{\text {th }}[/latex] trial head must appears. So required probability [latex] \begin{aligned} &={ }^{9} C_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{9} \times \frac{1}{2} \\ &=\frac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{3 !} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{10}=\frac{84}{1024}=0.082 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Given the vector [latex]A=(cos x)(sin y)\hat{a}_{x}+(sin x)(cos y)\hat{a}_{y} [/latex], where [latex] \hat{a}_{x},\hat{a}_{y}[/latex] denotes unit vectors along x , y directions, respectively. The magnitude of curl of A is____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{A}&=(\cos x)(\sin y) \hat{a}_{x}+(\sin x)(\cos y) \hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{A}&=(\cos x)(\sin y) \hat{a}_{x}+(\sin x)(\cos y) \hat{a}_{y}+0 \hat{a}_{z} & \hat{a}_{y} & \hat{a}_{z} \\ \nabla \times \vec{A}&=\left|\begin{array}{cccc} \hat{a}_{x} & \hat{a}_{y}&\hat{a}_{z}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ \cos x \sin y & \sin x \cos y & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ &=\hat{a}_{z}[\cos x \cos y-\cos x \cos y]=0 \\ \therefore|\nabla \times \vec{A}| &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The magnitude of the gradient for the function [latex]f(x,y,z)=x^{2}+3y^{2}+z^{3}[/latex] at the point (1,1,1) is _____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(v, y, z) &=x^{3}+3 y^{2}+z^{3} \\ \nabla f &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \hat{k} \\ &=2 x \hat{i}+6 y \hat{j}+3 z^{2} \hat{k} \\ (\Delta t)_{(1,1,1)} &=2 \hat{i}+6 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k} \\ |\Delta+|_{(1,1,1)} &=\sqrt{4+36+9}=\sqrt{49}=7 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.explanation: Given data: [latex] \begin{array}{l} i_{1}=2 \mathrm{A}, i_{4}=-1 \mathrm{A}, i_{5}=-4 \mathrm{A} \\ R=1 \Omega \end{array}[/latex] To calculate: [latex] i_{6}=?[/latex] Using KVL at all the three nodes we get, At node A [latex] i_{5}-i_{3}+i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(i)[/latex] At node B [latex] i_{4}+i_{1}-i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(ii)[/latex] At node C [latex] i_{6}+i_{3}-i_{1}=0 \qquad \ldots(iii)[/latex] By putting the value of [latex]i_{3}[/latex] and [latex]i_{2}[/latex] from equation (i) and (ii) in equation (iii) we get, [latex] \begin{aligned} i_{6}+\left(i_{2}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ i_{6}+\left(i_{1}+i_{4}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ \therefore \quad i_{6}+(2-1-4)-2&=0 \\ i_{6}&=5 \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:

[latex] \begin{array}{l} i_{1}=2 \mathrm{A}, i_{4}=-1 \mathrm{A}, i_{5}=-4 \mathrm{A} \\ R=1 \Omega \end{array}[/latex]

[latex] i_{6}=?[/latex]


Using KVL at all the three nodes we get,
At node A
[latex] i_{5}-i_{3}+i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(i)[/latex]
At node B
[latex] i_{4}+i_{1}-i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(ii)[/latex]
At node C
[latex] i_{6}+i_{3}-i_{1}=0 \qquad \ldots(iii)[/latex]
By putting the value of [latex]i_{3}[/latex] and [latex]i_{2}[/latex] from equation (i)
and (ii) in equation (iii) we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} i_{6}+\left(i_{2}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ i_{6}+\left(i_{1}+i_{4}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ \therefore \quad i_{6}+(2-1-4)-2&=0 \\ i_{6}&=5 \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
A continuous, linear time-invariant filter has an impulse response h(t) described
by [latex]h(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} 3 &for \; 0\leq t\leq 3 \\ 0&otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] When a constant input of values 5 is applied to this filter, the steady state output is_____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}3, & \text { for } 0 \leq t \leq 3 \\0, & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right.\\ h(t) &=3[u(t)-u(t-3)] \\ H(s) &=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \\ \therefore \quad x(t) &=5 \\ \text { Then } x(s) &=\frac{5}{s} \end{aligned}[/latex] We know that [latex] Y(s)=H(s) X(s)=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \cdot \frac{5}{s} [/latex] Steady state output [latex] \begin{array}{l} =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot \frac{15}{s} \frac{\left(1-e^{-3 s}\right)}{s} \\ =15 \cdot \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} 3 e^{-3 s} \quad[\because \quad \text { L-Hospital's rule }] \\ \quad=45 \end{array}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}3, & \text { for } 0 \leq t \leq 3 \\0, & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right.\\ h(t) &=3[u(t)-u(t-3)] \\ H(s) &=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \\ \therefore \quad x(t) &=5 \\ \text { Then } x(s) &=\frac{5}{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that
[latex] Y(s)=H(s) X(s)=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \cdot \frac{5}{s} [/latex]
Steady state output
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot \frac{15}{s} \frac{\left(1-e^{-3 s}\right)}{s} \\ =15 \cdot \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} 3 e^{-3 s} \quad[\because \quad \text { L-Hospital's rule }] \\ \quad=45 \end{array}[/latex]

questions.question:
A two-port network has scattering parameters given by [latex][S]=\begin{bmatrix} S_{11} &S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex].  If the
port-2 of the two port is short circuited, the [latex]S_{11}[/latex]
 parameter for the resultant one port network is
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{array}{l} b_{1}=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12} \cdot a_{2} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ b_{2}=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2}\qquad\ldots(ii) \end{array}[/latex] When output is short, [latex]a_{2}=-b_{2} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} -a_{2} &=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{2} &=\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex] Substituting in first equation, [latex] \begin{aligned} b_{1} &=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12}\left(\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}}\right) \\ &=\frac{s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22} a_{1}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21} a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}} &=s_{11}=\frac{s_{11}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} b_{1}=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12} \cdot a_{2} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ b_{2}=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2}\qquad\ldots(ii) \end{array}[/latex]
When output is short, [latex]a_{2}=-b_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} -a_{2} &=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{2} &=\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in first equation,
[latex] \begin{aligned} b_{1} &=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12}\left(\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}}\right) \\ &=\frac{s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22} a_{1}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21} a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}} &=s_{11}=\frac{s_{11}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

The digital logic shown in the figure satisfies the given state diagram when [latex]Q_{1}[/latex] is connected to input A of the XOR gate. Suppose the XOR gate is replaced by an XNOR gate. Which one of the following
options preserves the state diagram ?

When replaced by X-NOR gate Now [latex]D_{2}=A \odot S [/latex] Also, we know that [latex] \overline{A \oplus B}= \overline{A} \oplus B=A \odot B [/latex] We require output to be as [latex]D_{2}=A \oplus S [/latex] So, to keep this output, A should be connected to [latex] \bar{Q}_{1}[/latex] as [latex] D_{2}=\overline{Q}_{1} \odot S=\overline{Q_{1} \odot S}=Q_{1} \oplus S[/latex]

Initially when X-OR gate is connected to the input of flip flop 2 i.e. input of [latex]D_{2}[/latex] , i.e.
[latex] D_{2}=A \oplus S=Q_{1} \oplus S[/latex]
Now, X-OR is replaced by X-NOR, keeping state diagram to be unchanged it means the input to [latex] D_{2}[/latex] should not get changed.
When replaced by X-NOR gate
Now [latex]D_{2}=A \odot S [/latex]
Also, we know that

questions.question:
Consider a discrete time periodic signal [latex]x[n]=sin(\frac{\pi n}{5})[/latex]. Let [latex]a_{k}[/latex] be the complex Fourier series coefficients of x[n]. The coefficients [latex]\{a_{k}\}[/latex] are non-zero when
k = Bm[latex]{\pm }[/latex]1, where m is any integer. The value of B is ____.
questions.explanation: From discrete Fourier series definition [latex] \begin{array}{l} x[n]=\sum_{K=0}^{N-1} a_{K} e^{j K\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}\right) n}\\ =a_{-1} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}+a_{0}+a_{1} e^{i \frac{2 \pi}{N} n} \quad \ldots(i)\\ x[n]=\frac{-1}{2 j} e^{-i \frac{\pi}{5} n}+\frac{1}{2 j} e^{i \frac{\pi}{5} n} \end{array}[/latex] Also given [latex] x[n]=\sin \left(\frac{\pi n}{5}\right) [/latex] where [latex] N=10\left[\frac{2 \pi}{N}=\frac{\pi}{5} \Rightarrow N=10\right] [/latex] By comparison [latex]a_{1}=\frac{1}{2 j} and a_{9}=a_{-1}=\frac{-1}{2 j} [/latex] As the TFS coefficient [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is also periodic with period N=10. [latex] \begin{aligned} a_{1} &=a_{11}=a_{21} \cdots \\ a_{-1} &=a_{9}=a_{19} \cdots \end{aligned}[/latex] Given that [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is non-zero for [latex]K=B m \pm 1 [/latex] [latex] \begin{array}{cc} B m \pm 1=1& \quad 9 \cdots\\ -1 &\quad11\ldots\\ \text{For }m=0 \quad for& \quad m=1 \\ \end{array}[/latex] To satisfy this condition B must be '10' where 'm'  is any integer.
questions.explanation_html:
From discrete Fourier series definition
[latex] \begin{array}{l} x[n]=\sum_{K=0}^{N-1} a_{K} e^{j K\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}\right) n}\\ =a_{-1} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}+a_{0}+a_{1} e^{i \frac{2 \pi}{N} n} \quad \ldots(i)\\ x[n]=\frac{-1}{2 j} e^{-i \frac{\pi}{5} n}+\frac{1}{2 j} e^{i \frac{\pi}{5} n} \end{array}[/latex]
Also given
[latex] x[n]=\sin \left(\frac{\pi n}{5}\right) [/latex]
where [latex] N=10\left[\frac{2 \pi}{N}=\frac{\pi}{5} \Rightarrow N=10\right] [/latex]
By comparison [latex]a_{1}=\frac{1}{2 j} and a_{9}=a_{-1}=\frac{-1}{2 j} [/latex]
As the TFS coefficient [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is also periodic with period N=10.
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{1} &=a_{11}=a_{21} \cdots \\ a_{-1} &=a_{9}=a_{19} \cdots \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is non-zero for [latex]K=B m \pm 1 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{cc} B m \pm 1=1& \quad 9 \cdots\\ -1 &\quad11\ldots\\ \text{For }m=0 \quad for& \quad m=1 \\ \end{array}[/latex]
To satisfy this condition B must be '10' where 'm' is any integer.

questions.question:
A system is described by the following differential equation, where u(t) is the
input to the system and y(t) is the output of the system. [latex]\dot{y}(t)+5y(t)=u(t)[/latex] when y(0) = 1 and u(t)  is a unit step function, y(t)  is
questions.explanation: [latex]\dot{y}(t)+5 y(t)=u(t) [/latex] Taking the Laplace transform of the above equation [latex] \begin{aligned} s Y(s)-y(0)+5 & r(s)=\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+5) r(s)-1 & =\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+5) r(s) & =\frac{s+1}{s} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{(s+1)}{s(s+5)} \\ \frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+5)} & =\frac{(s+1)}{s(s+5)} \\ A&=0.2 \\ B&=\frac{-4}{-5}=0.8 \\ r(s) &=\frac{0.2}{s}+\frac{0.8}{(s+5)}\\ y(t)&=0.2+0.8 e^{-5 t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
For the following feedback system [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex]. The 2% settling time of the step response is required to be less than 2 seconds.
Which one of the following compensators C(s) achieves this ?
questions.explanation: Given open loop transfer function is [latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} \\ \therefore T(s)&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)+1} \\ T(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+3 s+3} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Comparing equation (i) with standard transfer function [latex] \xi \omega_{n}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 [/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] 2% settling time [latex] \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{1.5}=2.67>2 \mathrm{sec} [/latex] Thus, in order to make settling time [latex]\left(\tau_{s}\right)[/latex] less than 2 sec, PD controller should be used. Hence, option (C) is the correct choice. Where, [latex]C(s)=2(s+4) [/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] New transfer function [latex]=T^{\prime}(G)[/latex] [latex] =\frac{C(s) G(s)}{1+C(s) G(s)}=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+3 s+2+2 s+8} [/latex] or [latex]T^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+5 s+10}[/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{5 / 2}=\frac{4}{2.5}=1.6[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given open loop transfer function is
[latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} \\ \therefore T(s)&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)+1} \\ T(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+3 s+3} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing equation (i) with standard transfer function
[latex] \xi \omega_{n}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] 2% settling time
[latex] \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{1.5}=2.67>2 \mathrm{sec} [/latex]
Thus, in order to make settling time [latex]\left(\tau_{s}\right)[/latex] less than 2 sec, PD controller should be used. Hence, option (C) is the correct choice.
Where, [latex]C(s)=2(s+4) [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] New transfer function [latex]=T^{\prime}(G)[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{C(s) G(s)}{1+C(s) G(s)}=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+3 s+2+2 s+8} [/latex]
or [latex]T^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+5 s+10}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{5 / 2}=\frac{4}{2.5}=1.6[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a random process [latex]X(t)=\sqrt{2}sin(2\pi t+\varphi )[/latex], where the random phase [latex]\varphi[/latex] is uniformly distributed in the interval [latex][0, 2\pi ][/latex] . The auto-correlation [latex]E[X(t_{1})X(t_{2})][/latex] is
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \left.E\left[X\left(t_{1}\right) X\left(t_{1}\right)\right]=E\left[A \sin \left(2 \pi t_{1}+\phi\right)\right] \times A \sin \left(2 \pi t_{2}+\phi\right)\right] \\ =\frac{A^{2}}{2} E\left[\cos \left[2 \pi\left(t_{1}-t_{2}\right)\right]-\cos \left[2 \pi\left(t_{1}+t_{2}+2 \phi\right)\right]\right. \\ =\frac{A^{2}}{2} \cos \left[2 \pi\left(t_{1}-t_{2}\right)\right. \end{array}[/latex]

questions.question:
Let [latex]Q(\sqrt{\gamma })[/latex] be the BER of a BPSK system over an AWGN channel with twosided noise power spectral density [latex]N_{0}/2[/latex]. The parameter [latex]\gamma [/latex] is a function of bit energy and noise power spectral density. A system with two independent and identical AWGN channels with noise power
spectral density [latex]N_{0}/2[/latex]  is shown in the figure. The BPSK demodulator receives the sum of outputs of both the channels. If the BER of this system is  [latex]Q(b\sqrt{\gamma })[/latex] , then the value of  [latex]b[/latex] is
questions.explanation: since the same signal is passed through two  parallel channels and added at the receiver input, the effective distance between the adjacent message points will be [latex]d_{\min }=4 \sqrt{E_{b}}[/latex] and the  effective noise PSD(one-sided) will be [latex] N_{\alpha \text { ett }}=2 N_{o} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So},\quad B E R &=Q(\sqrt{\frac{d_{\min }^{2}}{2 N_{o(\mathrm{etl})}}})=Q(\sqrt{\frac{16 E_{D}}{4 N_{o}}}) \\ &=Q(\sqrt{4 \frac{E_{b}}{N_{0}}})=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{0}}}) \end{aligned}[/latex] For single channel case. [latex] \mathrm{BER}=\alpha(\sqrt{\gamma})=Q(\sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{o}}})[/latex] So, for the given problem, [latex] \begin{aligned} B E R=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{0}}})&=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\gamma})=Q(b \sqrt{\gamma}) \\ \text{So, }\quad b=\sqrt{2}&=1.414 \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
since the same signal is passed through two parallel channels and added at the receiver input, the effective distance between the adjacent message points will be [latex]d_{\min }=4 \sqrt{E_{b}}[/latex] and the effective noise PSD(one-sided) will be [latex] N_{\alpha \text { ett }}=2 N_{o} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So},\quad B E R &=Q(\sqrt{\frac{d_{\min }^{2}}{2 N_{o(\mathrm{etl})}}})=Q(\sqrt{\frac{16 E_{D}}{4 N_{o}}}) \\ &=Q(\sqrt{4 \frac{E_{b}}{N_{0}}})=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{0}}}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
For single channel case.
[latex] \mathrm{BER}=\alpha(\sqrt{\gamma})=Q(\sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{o}}})[/latex]
So, for the given problem,
[latex] \begin{aligned} B E R=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 E_{b}}{N_{0}}})&=Q(\sqrt{2} \sqrt{\gamma})=Q(b \sqrt{\gamma}) \\ \text{So, }\quad b=\sqrt{2}&=1.414 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until a 'Head' appears for the first time. Let
L be the number of tosses to get this first ' Head' . The entropy H (L) in bits is
_____.
questions.explanation: If P=1, i.e. if 1 toss is required to gets first head. Then probability to get the first head [latex] \Rightarrow \quad P_{1}=\frac{1}{2} [/latex] If P=2; i.e. if 2 tosses are required to get first head. Then probability to get the first head [latex] \Rightarrow \quad P_{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4} [/latex] If P=3; i.e. if 3 tosses are required to get first head. Then probability to get the first head [latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \quad P_{3}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8} \\ \text { Entropy } H=\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i} \log _{2} \frac{1}{P_{i}} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 2}+\frac{1}{4} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 4}+\log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 8}+\frac{1}{16} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 16} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \times 1+\frac{1}{4} \times 2+\frac{1}{8} \times 3+\frac{1}{16} \times 4+\cdots \\ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{(2)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(2)^{3}}+\frac{4}{(2)^{4}}+\cdots \\ H \simeq 2 \end{array}[/latex]

If P=3; i.e. if 3 tosses are required to get first head.
Then probability to get the first head
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \quad P_{3}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8} \\ \text { Entropy } H=\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i} \log _{2} \frac{1}{P_{i}} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 2}+\frac{1}{4} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 4}+\log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 8}+\frac{1}{16} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 16} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \times 1+\frac{1}{4} \times 2+\frac{1}{8} \times 3+\frac{1}{16} \times 4+\cdots \\ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{(2)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(2)^{3}}+\frac{4}{(2)^{4}}+\cdots \\ H \simeq 2 \end{array}[/latex]

questions.question:
In spherical coordinates, let [latex]\hat{a}_{\theta },\hat{a}_{\phi }[/latex]
 denote unit vectors along the [latex]\theta, \phi[/latex]  directions. [latex]E=\frac{100}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\theta V/m[/latex] and [latex]E=\frac{0.265}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\phi A/m[/latex] represent the electric and magnetic field components of the EM wave at large
distances [latex]r[/latex]  from a dipole antenna, in free space. The average power (W) crossing
the hemispherical shell located at r = 1 km, [latex]0\leq \theta \leq \pi /2[/latex] is ____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E} &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{100}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\theta} V / m \\ &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{0.265}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta \beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\phi} V / m \end{aligned}[/latex] Poynting vector, [latex] \vec{P}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{Re}\left[\vec{E} \times \vec{H}^{*}\right]=\frac{26.5}{2 r^{2}} \sin ^{2} \theta \hat{a}_{r} W / m^{2}[/latex] The average power crossing the given hemispherical shell is, [latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Power } &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \vec{P} \cdot r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \hat{a}_{r} \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^{3} \theta d \theta \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \frac{2}{3}=55.5 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E} &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{100}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\theta} V / m \\ &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{0.265}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta \beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\phi} V / m \end{aligned}[/latex]
Poynting vector,
[latex] \vec{P}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{Re}\left[\vec{E} \times \vec{H}^{*}\right]=\frac{26.5}{2 r^{2}} \sin ^{2} \theta \hat{a}_{r} W / m^{2}[/latex]
The average power crossing the given
hemispherical shell is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Power } &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \vec{P} \cdot r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \hat{a}_{r} \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^{3} \theta d \theta \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \frac{2}{3}=55.5 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
For a parallel plate transmission line, let v be the speed of propagation and Z
be the characteristic impedance. Neglecting fringe effects, a reduction of the
spacing between the plates by a factor of two results in

options.A: halving of v and no change in Z
options.B: no changes in v and halving of Z
options.C: no change in both v and Z
options.D: halving of both v and Z

questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{0}&=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} \text{ for parallel plate line}\\ \frac{C}{l}&=\frac{\epsilon W}{d} \text{ and } \frac{L}{l}=\frac{\mu d}{W} \\ \text{where}, \quad W&= \text{Width of the line}\\ d &=\text { Separation between the lines } \\ Z_{0} & \propto d \quad (Z_{0}\text{ change by half})\\ \text { Velocity } &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L C}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0} \epsilon_{0}}}=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}\\ &\qquad\text{(No change in V)} \end{aligned}\\[/latex]

questions.question: The input impedance of a [latex]\frac{\lambda }{8}[/latex] section of a lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] is found to be real when the other end is terminated by a load [latex]Z_{L}=(R+jX)\Omega[/latex]. If X is  30 [latex]\Omega[/latex], the value of R(in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) is_____.

questions.question:
Consider the periodic square wave in the figure shown. The ratio of the power in the [latex]7^{th}[/latex] harmonic to the power in the [latex]5^{th}[/latex] harmonic for
this waveform is closest in value to ______.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} X(\omega) &=\sum_{K=-\infty}^{\infty} 2 \pi a_{k} \delta\left(0-K \omega\right) \\ a_{K} &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2} x(t) e^{-j K \omega_{0} t} d t \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{2 \pi}\left\{\int_{0}^{1} 1 \cdot e^{-j K \omega_{o} t} d \omega-\int_{1}^{2} 1 \cdot e^{-j K \omega_{o} t} d \omega\right\}\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\frac{1}{-j K \omega_{o}}[e^{-j K \omega_{o}}-1]-\frac{1}{-j K \omega_{o}}[e^{(-j 2K \omega_{o})}-e^{(-j 2K \omega_{o})}] \right ]\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\frac{e^{-j K \omega_{o}l2}}{j K \omega_{o}}.2j\sin\frac{K\omega_{o}}{2}-\frac{1}{j K \omega_{o}}e^{-\frac{j K \omega_{o}3}{2}}\left(2j\sin\frac{K\omega_{0}}{2} \right ) \right ]\\ &=\frac{1}{\pi}\left[\frac{\sin \frac{K \omega_{o}}{2}}{K \omega_{o}}\left(e^{-j K \omega_{0}}\right)\left(e^{\frac{j K \omega_{0}}{2}}-e^{-\frac{K_{m_{2}}}{2}}\right)\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{\sin K \omega_{0} / 2}{K \omega_{o}}\right) e^{-j K \omega_{0}} \times 2 j \sin \left(\frac{\left.K_{\left(0_{0}\right.}\right)}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}} \frac{\left(\sin K \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2}}{K} 2 j \times \cos K \pi \end{aligned}\\[/latex] [latex]7^{\text {th }}[/latex] harmonic power [latex]=\left(2 \pi a_{7}\right)^{2} [/latex] [latex] 5^{\text {th }}[/latex] harmonic power [latex]=\left(2 \pi a_{5}\right)^{2} [/latex] [latex] Ratio =\left(\frac{a_{7}}{a_{5}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^{2}=\frac{25}{49}=0.51[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} X(\omega) &=\sum_{K=-\infty}^{\infty} 2 \pi a_{k} \delta\left(0-K \omega\right) \\ a_{K} &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2} x(t) e^{-j K \omega_{0} t} d t \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{1}{2 \pi}\left\{\int_{0}^{1} 1 \cdot e^{-j K \omega_{o} t} d \omega-\int_{1}^{2} 1 \cdot e^{-j K \omega_{o} t} d \omega\right\}\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\frac{1}{-j K \omega_{o}}[e^{-j K \omega_{o}}-1]-\frac{1}{-j K \omega_{o}}[e^{(-j 2K \omega_{o})}-e^{(-j 2K \omega_{o})}] \right ]\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\frac{e^{-j K \omega_{o}l2}}{j K \omega_{o}}.2j\sin\frac{K\omega_{o}}{2}-\frac{1}{j K \omega_{o}}e^{-\frac{j K \omega_{o}3}{2}}\left(2j\sin\frac{K\omega_{0}}{2} \right ) \right ]\\ &=\frac{1}{\pi}\left[\frac{\sin \frac{K \omega_{o}}{2}}{K \omega_{o}}\left(e^{-j K \omega_{0}}\right)\left(e^{\frac{j K \omega_{0}}{2}}-e^{-\frac{K_{m_{2}}}{2}}\right)\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{\sin K \omega_{0} / 2}{K \omega_{o}}\right) e^{-j K \omega_{0}} \times 2 j \sin \left(\frac{\left.K_{\left(0_{0}\right.}\right)}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{\pi^{2}} \frac{\left(\sin K \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2}}{K} 2 j \times \cos K \pi \end{aligned}\\[/latex]
[latex]7^{\text {th }}[/latex] harmonic power [latex]=\left(2 \pi a_{7}\right)^{2} [/latex]
[latex] 5^{\text {th }}[/latex] harmonic power [latex]=\left(2 \pi a_{5}\right)^{2} [/latex]
[latex] Ratio =\left(\frac{a_{7}}{a_{5}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^{2}=\frac{25}{49}=0.51[/latex]

is given by [latex]C=Wlog_{2}(1+\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}W})[/latex] bits per second (bps), where W is the channel bandwidth, P is the average power received and [latex]{\sigma^{2}}[/latex] is the one sided power spectral density of the AWGN. For a fixed [latex]\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}}=1000[/latex], the channel capacity (in kbps) with infinite bandwidth [latex](W\rightarrow \infty )[/latex] is approximately.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} C&=W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right) \\ C&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \times \frac{\sigma^{2}}{P} W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{when }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty \\ C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \lim _{w \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{as }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty, \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}\text{ also }\rightarrow \infty \\ \therefore C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \frac{\lim _{\alpha} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}}\right)}{P} \\ &\quad \left[\because \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} x \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)=\log\right]\\ C_{\infty} &=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \log _{2} e\\ C_{\infty} &=1.44\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} Y_{2}=&\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1 \end{array}\right] \\ \text { Thus, } \quad Y=Y_{1}+Y_{2}=&\left[\begin{array}{cc} \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{5}{6} \\ -\frac{5}{6} & \frac{5}{3} \end{array}\right] \\ \therefore \quad I_{1}=& Y_{11} V_{1}+Y_{12} V_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{5}{3} Y_{1}-\frac{5}{6} V_{2} &\ldots(i)\\ I_{2} &=Y_{21} V_{1}+Y_{22} V_{2} \\ &=-\frac{5}{6} V_{1}+\frac{5}{3} V_{2} &\ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad h_{22} &=\left.\frac{I_{2}}{V_{2}}\right|_{I_{1}=0} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] From equation (i), we get, [latex] V_{1}=\frac{1}{2} V_{2} \qquad \ldots(iii)[/latex] and from equation (ii) and (iii), we get, [latex] h_{22}=\frac{I_{2}}{V_{2}}=\frac{15}{12}=1.25[/latex]

Similarly for network (2).
[latex] \begin{aligned} Y_{2}=&\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1 \end{array}\right] \\ \text { Thus, } \quad Y=Y_{1}+Y_{2}=&\left[\begin{array}{cc} \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{5}{6} \\ -\frac{5}{6} & \frac{5}{3} \end{array}\right] \\ \therefore \quad I_{1}=& Y_{11} V_{1}+Y_{12} V_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=\frac{5}{3} Y_{1}-\frac{5}{6} V_{2} &\ldots(i)\\ I_{2} &=Y_{21} V_{1}+Y_{22} V_{2} \\ &=-\frac{5}{6} V_{1}+\frac{5}{3} V_{2} &\ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad h_{22} &=\left.\frac{I_{2}}{V_{2}}\right|_{I_{1}=0} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a discrete-time signal [latex]x[n]=\left\{\begin{matrix} n & for \; 0\leq n\leq 10\\ 0&otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] If y[n] is the convolution of x[n] with itself, the value of y[4] is _____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{array}{l} x[n]=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} n & \text { for } 0 \leq n \leq 10 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right. \\ y[n]=\sum_{K=\infty}^{\infty} x(k) x(n-k) \\ y[4]=\sum_{k=0}^{10} x(k) x(4-k) \\ =x(0) x(4)+x(1) x(3)+x(2) x(2)+x(3) x(1)+0 \\ =0+(1 \times 3)+(2 \times 2)+(3 \times 1) \\ =10 \end{array}[/latex]

questions.question: The input-output relationship of a causal stable LTI system is given as [latex]y[n] = \alpha[/latex] y[n -1]+ [latex]\beta x[n][/latex] If the impulse response h[n] of this system satisfies the condition [latex]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }h[n]=2[/latex],  the relationship between [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] is
questions.explanation: Input-output relation is given as [latex] \begin{aligned} y[n]&=\alpha_{\mathcal{Y}}(n-1)+\beta x[n] \\ \text{Taking Z-transform, }\\ r(z)&=\alpha z^{-1} \quad Y (z)+\beta X(z) \\ Y(z)&\left[1-\alpha z^{-1}\right]=\beta X(z) \\ \frac{\gamma(z)}{X(z)}&=H(z)=\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha z^{-1}} \\ h[n]&=\beta \cdot \alpha^{n} u[n] \\ \text{Also }&\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h[n]=2 \Rightarrow \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \beta \cdot \alpha^{n} u[n]=2 \\ \frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}&=2 \Rightarrow \beta=2-2 \alpha \\ \Rightarrow 2 a &=2-\beta \\ \alpha &=1-\frac{\beta}{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

questions.question: An unforced linear time invariant (LTI) system is represented by [latex]\begin{vmatrix} \dot{x}_{1}\\ \dot{x}_{2} \end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 0&-2 \end{vmatrix}\begin{vmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{vmatrix}[/latex] If the initial conditions are [latex]x_{1}(0)=1 \; and \; x_{2}(0)=-1[/latex], the solution of the state equation is
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned}\left[\begin{array}{l}\dot{x}_{1} \\ \dot{x}_{2}\end{array}\right] &=\left[\begin{array}{cc}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{array}\right] \\ \dot{x}_{1} &=-x_{1}+0 x_{2} \\ \dot{x}_{2} &=0 x_{1}-2 x_{2} \end{aligned} [/latex] Applying Laplace transform on both equations [latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow s X_{1}(s)-x_{1}(0)&=-X_{1}(s) \\ X_{1}(s)[s+1]&=X_{1}(0) \quad &\text{given }x_{1}(0)=1 \\ X_{1}(s)&=\frac{1}{s+1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad e^{-t}&=x_{1}(t)\\ \Rightarrow \quad s X_{2}(s)-X_{2}(0)&=-2 X_{2}(s) \\ (s+2) X_{2}(s)&=X_{2}(0) &X_{2}(0)=-1 \\ X_{2}(s)&=-\frac{1}{s+2} \\ x_{2}(t)&=-e^{-2 t} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Applying Laplace transform on both equations

questions.explanation: Assume quantization voltage is [latex]V_{T h} [/latex] For outputs of quantizer to have equal probability [latex] \begin{aligned} \rightarrow P\left(X S V_{T h}\right)=& P\left(X \geq V_{T h}\right) \\ \int_{0}^{v_{T}} f_{X}(x) d x &=\int_{V_{m}} f_{X}(x) d x \\ \int_{0}^{V} 2 e^{-2 x} d x &=\int_{V_{T h}}^{\infty} 2 e^{-2 x} d x \\ e^{-2 x V_{i h}} &=\frac{1}{2} \\ V_{T h} &=0.346 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
For a rectangular waveguide of internal dimensions [latex]a \times b(a \gt b)[/latex], the cur-off
frequency for the [latex]TE_{11}[/latex] mode is the arithmetic mean of the cut-off frequencies for [latex]TE_{10}[/latex] mode and [latex]TE_{20}[/latex] mode. If a = [latex]\sqrt{5}[/latex] cm, the value of b (in cm) is______.
questions.explanation: Cut-off frequency of a rectangular waveguide is [latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m \pi}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n\pi}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{10}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{20}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text { for } \quad T E_{11} &=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^{2}}+\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ \text { Given, } f_{C T_{11}} &=\frac{f_{C_{I E 10}}+f_{C I E_{20}}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{\frac{c}{2 a}+\frac{c}{a}}{2} \\ \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{1}{2 a}+\frac{1}{a}=\frac{3}{2 a} \\ \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}&=\frac{9}{4 a^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2} &=\frac{5}{4 a^{2}} \\ b &=\frac{2 a}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2 \times \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\ &=2 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Cut-off frequency of a rectangular waveguide is
[latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m \pi}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n\pi}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{10}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{20}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text { for } \quad T E_{11} &=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^{2}}+\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ \text { Given, } f_{C T_{11}} &=\frac{f_{C_{I E 10}}+f_{C I E_{20}}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{\frac{c}{2 a}+\frac{c}{a}}{2} \\ \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{1}{2 a}+\frac{1}{a}=\frac{3}{2 a} \\ \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}&=\frac{9}{4 a^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2} &=\frac{5}{4 a^{2}} \\ b &=\frac{2 a}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2 \times \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\ &=2 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Match the application to appropriate numerical method.

An unbiased coin is tossed an infinite number of times. The probability that the
fourth head appears at the tenth toss is
questions.explanation: It means 3-head appears in [latex]1^{\text {st }}[/latex] 9 trials. Probability of getting exactly 3 head in 1^{\text {st }} 9 trials [latex] \begin{aligned} &=\text{ Coefficient } p^{3}\text{ in }(4+p) 9 \\ \text{When, }&[\overline{p+q=1}] \\ &={ }^{9} C_{3} q^{6} p^{3}\\ \text{when, }\quad \rho&= \text{ probability of occure of head}\\ q &=\text { probability of occure of tail } \\ &={ }^{9} C_{3} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{6}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} \\ &={ }^{9} C_{3} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{9} \end{aligned}[/latex] and in [latex]10^{\text {th }}[/latex] trial head must appears. So required probability [latex] \begin{aligned} &={ }^{9} C_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{9} \times \frac{1}{2} \\ &=\frac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{3 !} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{10}=\frac{84}{1024}=0.082 \end{aligned}[/latex]

and in [latex]10^{\text {th }}[/latex] trial head must appears.

questions.question:
A series RC circuit is connected to a DC voltage source at time t = 0. The
relation between the source voltage [latex]V_{S}[/latex], the resistance R, the capacitance C, and the current [latex]i(t)[/latex] is given below : [latex]V_{S}=Ri(t)+\frac{1}{C}\int_{0}^{t}i(u)du[/latex] Which one of the following represents the current [latex]i(t)[/latex] ?
questions.explanation: Given that: [latex] V_{s}=R i(t)+\frac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{t} i(t) d t\qquad\ldots(i)[/latex] Using Laplace transform, [latex] \begin{aligned} \text { WS) }&=R I(s)+\frac{1}{C s} I(s) &\ldots(ii)\\ \text { or } I(s)&=\frac{V(s)}{\left(R+\frac{1}{C S}\right)} &\ldots(iii)\\ \text { For, } V(s)&=\frac{1}{s}&\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex] From equation (iii) and (iv), [latex] I(s)=\frac{C}{(R C s+1)}=\frac{1}{R\left(s+\frac{1}{R C}\right)}\qquad\ldots(v)[/latex] Using inverse Laplace transform in equation (v), we get, [latex] i(t)=\frac{1}{R} e^{-t / R C}[/latex] Thus, option (A) is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Given that:
[latex] V_{s}=R i(t)+\frac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{t} i(t) d t\qquad\ldots(i)[/latex]
Using Laplace transform,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { WS) }&=R I(s)+\frac{1}{C s} I(s) &\ldots(ii)\\ \text { or } I(s)&=\frac{V(s)}{\left(R+\frac{1}{C S}\right)} &\ldots(iii)\\ \text { For, } V(s)&=\frac{1}{s}&\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From equation (iii) and (iv),
[latex] I(s)=\frac{C}{(R C s+1)}=\frac{1}{R\left(s+\frac{1}{R C}\right)}\qquad\ldots(v)[/latex]
Using inverse Laplace transform in equation (v), we get,
[latex] i(t)=\frac{1}{R} e^{-t / R C}[/latex]
Thus, option (A) is correct.

questions.question:
Consider the multiplexer based logic circuit shown in the figure.
Which one of the following Boolean functions is realized by the circuit ?
questions.explanation: Using the state equation of the multiplexer, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} X&=\bar{S}_{1} \cdot W+S_{1} \bar{W}\\ \text{So, }\quad F&=\bar{S}_{2} \cdot X+S_{2} \bar{X} \\ &=\bar{S}_{2}\left(\bar{S}_{1} W+S_{1} \bar{W}\right)+S_{2}(\overline{\bar{S}_{1} W+S_{1} \bar{W}}) \\ &=\bar{S}_{1} \bar{S}_{2} W+S_{1} \bar{S}_{2} \bar{W}+S_{2} \bar{S}_{1} \bar{W}+S_{2} S_{1} W \\ F&=W \oplus S_{1} \oplus S_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Using the state equation of the multiplexer, we
get
[latex] \begin{aligned} X&=\bar{S}_{1} \cdot W+S_{1} \bar{W}\\ \text{So, }\quad F&=\bar{S}_{2} \cdot X+S_{2} \bar{X} \\ &=\bar{S}_{2}\left(\bar{S}_{1} W+S_{1} \bar{W}\right)+S_{2}(\overline{\bar{S}_{1} W+S_{1} \bar{W}}) \\ &=\bar{S}_{1} \bar{S}_{2} W+S_{1} \bar{S}_{2} \bar{W}+S_{2} \bar{S}_{1} \bar{W}+S_{2} S_{1} W \\ F&=W \oplus S_{1} \oplus S_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
The input [latex]-3e^{2t}u(t)[/latex], where u(t) is the unit step function, is applied to a
system with transfer function [latex]\frac{s-2}{s+3}[/latex]. If the initial value of the output is -2, then the value of the output at steady state is _____.
questions.explanation: Given, [latex] x(t)=-3 e^{-2 t} [/latex] Laplace transform of [latex] x(t) \longleftrightarrow X(s)[/latex] Where, [latex] \begin{aligned} X(s) &=\frac{-3}{s+2} \\ A \mid s 0, H(s) &=\frac{s-2}{(s+3)} \\ \therefore \quad Y(s) &=X(s) H(s) \\ \gamma(s) &=\frac{-3(s-2)}{(s+3)(s+2)} \end{aligned}[/latex] Using final value theorem, the steady state value of Y(s) is [latex] \begin{aligned} y(\infty) &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s Y(s) \\ &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given, [latex] x(t)=-3 e^{-2 t} [/latex]
Laplace transform of
[latex] x(t) \longleftrightarrow X(s)[/latex]
Where,
[latex] \begin{aligned} X(s) &=\frac{-3}{s+2} \\ A \mid s 0, H(s) &=\frac{s-2}{(s+3)} \\ \therefore \quad Y(s) &=X(s) H(s) \\ \gamma(s) &=\frac{-3(s-2)}{(s+3)(s+2)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using final value theorem, the steady state value
of Y(s) is
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(\infty) &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s Y(s) \\ &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly till both head and tail appear at least once. The
average number of tosses required is____.
questions.explanation: To get both head and Tail atleast once. We have to toss minimum two times. The random variable x represents first toss starting  with Head. [latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(x) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ E(x) &=\Sigma x \cdot P(x) & \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Y represents first toss starting with Tail. [latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline y & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(y) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] The average number of tosses required [latex] =E(x)+E(y)=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=3[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
To get both head and Tail atleast once. We have to toss minimum two times. The random variable x represents first toss starting with Head.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(x) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ E(x) &=\Sigma x \cdot P(x) & \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Y represents first toss starting with Tail.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline y & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(y) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] The average number of tosses required
[latex] =E(x)+E(y)=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=3[/latex]

questions.question:
In the circuit shown in the figure, the angular frequency [latex]\omega[/latex] (in rad/s), at which
the Norton equivalent impedance as seen from terminals [latex]b-b'[/latex] is purely resistive,
is _____.
questions.explanation: Finding [latex]Z_{N}[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{1 \times j 0.5 \omega}{1+j 0.5 \omega}+\frac{1}{j \omega}=\frac{j \omega}{2+j \omega}+\frac{1}{j \omega} \\ \text { or } Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{2-\omega^{2}+j \omega}{2 j \omega-\omega^{2}}&\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Rationalizing equation (i), we get, [latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{\left(2-\omega^{2}\right)+j \omega}{2 j \omega-\omega^{2}} \times \frac{-\omega^{2}-j 2 \omega}{-\omega^{2}-j 2 \omega} \\ &=-\frac{2 \omega^{2}+\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}+j \frac{\left(\omega^{3}-4 \omega\right)}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex] In order to have a purely resistive impedance [latex]Z_{\text {bb }}^{\prime} [/latex], the imaginary part of equation (ii) will be equaled to zero. [latex] \begin{aligned} &\therefore \frac{-4 \omega+\omega^{3}}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}=0\\ &\text{or}\quad \omega^{3}=4 \omega \\ &\text{or}\quad \omega=\sqrt{4}=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Finding [latex]Z_{N}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{1 \times j 0.5 \omega}{1+j 0.5 \omega}+\frac{1}{j \omega}=\frac{j \omega}{2+j \omega}+\frac{1}{j \omega} \\ \text { or } Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{2-\omega^{2}+j \omega}{2 j \omega-\omega^{2}}&\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Rationalizing equation (i), we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{b b}^{\prime} &=\frac{\left(2-\omega^{2}\right)+j \omega}{2 j \omega-\omega^{2}} \times \frac{-\omega^{2}-j 2 \omega}{-\omega^{2}-j 2 \omega} \\ &=-\frac{2 \omega^{2}+\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}+j \frac{\left(\omega^{3}-4 \omega\right)}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
In order to have a purely resistive impedance [latex]Z_{\text {bb }}^{\prime} [/latex], the imaginary part of equation (ii) will be equaled to zero.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &\therefore \frac{-4 \omega+\omega^{3}}{\omega^{4}+2 \omega^{2}}=0\\ &\text{or}\quad \omega^{3}=4 \omega \\ &\text{or}\quad \omega=\sqrt{4}=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The slope of the [latex]I_{D}[/latex] vs. [latex]V_{GS}[/latex] curve of an n-channel MOSFET in linear regime is [latex]10^{-3}\Omega ^{-1}[/latex] at [latex]V_{DS}[/latex] = 0.1V. questions.explanation: We known that for linear region, [latex] \begin{aligned} I_{D} &=K_{n}\left[\left(V_{G S}-V_{t}\right) V_{D S}-\frac{V_{D S}^{2}}{2}\right] \\ \frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{G S}} &=K_{n} V_{D S}\\ \frac{10^{-3}}{0.1}&=K_{n} \\ \text{i.e.} \quad K_{n}&=10^{-2} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] and for saturation region [latex] \begin{aligned} I_{D} &=\frac{K_{n}}{2}\left(V_{G S}-V_{t}\right)^{2} \\ \sqrt{I_{D}} &=\sqrt{\frac{K_{n}}{2}}\left(V_{G S}-V_{t}\right) \\ \frac{\partial \sqrt{I_{D}}}{\partial V_{G S}} &=\sqrt{\frac{K_{n}}{2}}\\ \text{So }\quad\frac{\partial \sqrt{I_{D}}}{\partial V_{G S}}&=\sqrt{\frac{10^{-2}}{2}}=0.0707 \frac{\sqrt{A}}{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

We known that for linear region,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{D} &=K_{n}\left[\left(V_{G S}-V_{t}\right) V_{D S}-\frac{V_{D S}^{2}}{2}\right] \\ \frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{G S}} &=K_{n} V_{D S}\\ \frac{10^{-3}}{0.1}&=K_{n} \\ \text{i.e.} \quad K_{n}&=10^{-2} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
Let [latex]H_{1}(z)=(1-pz^{-1})^{-1}[/latex], [latex]H_{2}(z)=(1-qz^{-1})^{-1}[/latex], [latex]H(z)=H_{1}(z)+rH_{2}(z)[/latex]. The

questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Here } H_1(z)&=\frac{1}{1-pz^{-1}} \\ H_2(z)&= \frac{1}{1-qz^{-1}}\\ \text{also } p&=\frac{1}{2},\; q=-\frac{1}{4} \\ \therefore \; H(z)&=H_1(z)+rH_2(z) \\ &= \frac{1}{1-pz^{-1}}+\frac{r}{1-qz^{-1}}\\ &= \frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}+\frac{r}{1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1}}\\ H(z)&=\frac{\left ( 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1} \right )+r\left ( 1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1} \right )}{\left ( 1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1} \right )}\;\;...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] zero of [latex]H(z) \Rightarrow [/latex] [latex] (1+r)-(q+p r) z^{-1}=0 \; \; ...(ii)[/latex] or [latex]\quad z=\frac{q+p r}{1+r} [/latex] Since, the zero of H(z) lies on the unit circle therefore [latex]|z|=1[/latex] or [latex] z=\pm 1 [/latex] Taking z=1, we get [latex] z=\frac{q+p r}{1+r}=1 \; \; ...(iii)[/latex] By solving above expression with [latex]p=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] and [latex] q=-\frac{1}{4},[/latex] we get [latex] r=-2.5[/latex] But [latex]|r| \lt 1 \quad [/latex] or [latex]\quad-1 \lt r \lt 1 [/latex] Taking z=-1 in equation (iii), we get [latex] r=-0.5[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Here } H_1(z)&=\frac{1}{1-pz^{-1}} \\ H_2(z)&= \frac{1}{1-qz^{-1}}\\ \text{also } p&=\frac{1}{2},\; q=-\frac{1}{4} \\ \therefore \; H(z)&=H_1(z)+rH_2(z) \\ &= \frac{1}{1-pz^{-1}}+\frac{r}{1-qz^{-1}}\\ &= \frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1}}+\frac{r}{1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1}}\\ H(z)&=\frac{\left ( 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1} \right )+r\left ( 1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1} \right )}{\left ( 1-\frac{1}{2}z^{-1} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{1}{4}z^{-1} \right )}\;\;...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
zero of [latex]H(z) \Rightarrow [/latex]
[latex] (1+r)-(q+p r) z^{-1}=0 \; \; ...(ii)[/latex]
or [latex]\quad z=\frac{q+p r}{1+r} [/latex]
Since, the zero of H(z) lies on the unit circle
therefore [latex]|z|=1[/latex] or [latex] z=\pm 1 [/latex]
Taking z=1, we get
[latex] z=\frac{q+p r}{1+r}=1 \; \; ...(iii)[/latex]
By solving above expression with [latex]p=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] and [latex] q=-\frac{1}{4},[/latex] we get
[latex] r=-2.5[/latex]
But [latex]|r| \lt 1 \quad [/latex] or [latex]\quad-1 \lt r \lt 1 [/latex]
Taking z=-1 in equation (iii), we get
[latex] r=-0.5[/latex]

questions.question: The state equation of a second-order linear system is given by [latex]\dot{x}(t) = Ax(t), \;\; x(0) = x_{0}[/latex] For  [latex]x_{0}=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \; x(t)=\begin{bmatrix} e^{-t}\\ -e^{-t} \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and  for [latex] x_{0}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix},[/latex] [latex] x(t)=\begin{bmatrix} e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\\ -e^{-t}+2e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix} [/latex] when  [latex] x_{0}=\begin{bmatrix} 3\\ 5 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], x(t) is
questions.explanation: Given [latex]\dot{x}(t)=A x(t), \quad x(0)=x_{0} [/latex] Taking the Laplace transform [latex] \begin{aligned} s X(s)-x(0) &=A X(s) \\ [s I-A] X(s) &=x(0) \\ X(s) &=[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) \\ x(t) &=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Condition given are [latex] \begin{aligned} For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{c}e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t}\end{array}\right] \\ For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{l}e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t}\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex] Using the linearity property in equation (i) [latex] K_{1} x_{1}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{1}(0) K_{1} [/latex] [latex] K_{2} x_{2}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{2}(0) K_{2} [/latex] Using the linearity property as [latex] \begin{aligned} K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t)&=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} \\  \left[K_{1} x_{1}(0)+K_{2} x_{2}(0)\right] & \quad \ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad X_{3}(s)&=[s I-A]^{-1} x_{3}(0) \\ \text{So, } \quad K_{1}\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]+&K_{2}\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \left[\begin{array}{l}K_{1}+O K_{2} \\ -K_{1}+K_{2}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{1}&=3 \\ K_{2}&=8 \end{aligned}[/latex] So, from equation (ii), we get x(t) [latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t) \\ &=3\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t} \end{array}\right]+8\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{c} 11 e^{-t}-8 e^{-2 t} \\ -1 t e^{-t}+16 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

Taking the Laplace transform
[latex] \begin{aligned} s X(s)-x(0) &=A X(s) \\ [s I-A] X(s) &=x(0) \\ X(s) &=[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) \\ x(t) &=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Condition given are
[latex] \begin{aligned} For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{c}e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t}\end{array}\right] \\ For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{l}e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t}\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using the linearity property in equation (i)
[latex] K_{1} x_{1}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{1}(0) K_{1} [/latex]
[latex] K_{2} x_{2}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{2}(0) K_{2} [/latex]
Using the linearity property as
[latex] \begin{aligned} K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t)&=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} \\ \left[K_{1} x_{1}(0)+K_{2} x_{2}(0)\right] & \quad \ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad X_{3}(s)&=[s I-A]^{-1} x_{3}(0) \\ \text{So, } \quad K_{1}\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]+&K_{2}\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \left[\begin{array}{l}K_{1}+O K_{2} \\ -K_{1}+K_{2}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{1}&=3 \\ K_{2}&=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, from equation (ii), we get x(t)
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t) \\ &=3\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t} \end{array}\right]+8\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{c} 11 e^{-t}-8 e^{-2 t} \\ -1 t e^{-t}+16 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question:
A binary random variable X takes the value of 1 with probability 1/3. X is
input to a cascade of 2 independent identical binary symmetric channels (BSCs) each with crossover probability 1/2. The output of BSCs are the random variables [latex]Y_{1}[/latex] and [latex]Y_{2}[/latex] as shown in the figure. The value of [latex]H(Y_{1})+ H(Y_{2})[/latex] in bits is ____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(X=1) &=\frac{1}{3} \text { and } P(X=0)=\frac{2}{3} \\ \text { and } \quad H\left(Y_{1}\right) &=P\left(Y_{1}\right) \log _{2} \frac{1}{P\left(Y_{1}\right)} \\ H\left(Y_{2}\right) &=P\left(Y_{2}\right) \log \frac{1}{P\left(Y_{2}\right)} \\ \text { where, } P\left(Y_{1}\right.&=1)=P\left(Y_{1}=0\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Similarly, [latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(Y_{2}=1\right)&=P\left(Y_{2}=0\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\ \text { Here } H\left(Y_{1}\right)+H\left(Y_{2}\right)&=\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2 \\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2 \\ H\left(Y_{1}\right)+H\left(Y_{2}\right)&=2 \text { bits } \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{A}&=(\cos x)(\sin y) \hat{a}_{x}+(\sin x)(\cos y) \hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{A}&=(\cos x)(\sin y) \hat{a}_{x}+(\sin x)(\cos y) \hat{a}_{y}+0 \hat{a}_{z} & \hat{a}_{y} & \hat{a}_{z} \\ \nabla \times \vec{A}&=\left|\begin{array}{cccc} \hat{a}_{x} & \hat{a}_{y}&\hat{a}_{z}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ \cos x \sin y & \sin x \cos y & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ &=\hat{a}_{z}[\cos x \cos y-\cos x \cos y]=0 \\ \therefore|\nabla \times \vec{A}| &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The magnitude of the gradient for the function [latex]f(x,y,z)=x^{2}+3y^{2}+z^{3}[/latex] at the point (1,1,1) is _____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(v, y, z) &=x^{3}+3 y^{2}+z^{3} \\ \nabla f &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \hat{k} \\ &=2 x \hat{i}+6 y \hat{j}+3 z^{2} \hat{k} \\ (\Delta t)_{(1,1,1)} &=2 \hat{i}+6 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k} \\ |\Delta+|_{(1,1,1)} &=\sqrt{4+36+9}=\sqrt{49}=7 \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(v, y, z) &=x^{3}+3 y^{2}+z^{3} \\ \nabla f &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \hat{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \hat{k} \\ &=2 x \hat{i}+6 y \hat{j}+3 z^{2} \hat{k} \\ (\Delta t)_{(1,1,1)} &=2 \hat{i}+6 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k} \\ |\Delta+|_{(1,1,1)} &=\sqrt{4+36+9}=\sqrt{49}=7 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Let X be a zero mean unit variance Gaussian random variable. E[|X|] is equal to ______.
questions.explanation: For a Gaussian random variable, [latex] \begin{aligned} f_{x}(x)&=\frac{1}{\sigma_{x} \sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\left(\frac{\mu-x}{2 \sigma^{2}}\right)^{2}} \\ \text{For mean} (\mu)&=0 \text{ and Variance }\left(\sigma_{x}^{2}\right)=1 \\ f_{X}(x) &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2}} \\ E[|x|] &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x| f_{X}(x) d x \\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x| \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x \\ =& \int_{-\infty}^{0}-x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{-x^{2}} d x+\int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x\\ &=2 \int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} x \cdot e^{\frac{-x^{2}}{2}} d x \\ &\text{Let }\quad -\frac{x^{2}}{2}=t \\ &\therefore \quad-\frac{2 x d x}{2}=d t \\ &\text{Hence }\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty}-e^{-t} d t=0.8 \\ &\therefore \quad E[|x|]=0.8 \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The circuit shown represents
In the circuit shown in the figure, if C = 0, the expression for Y is
questions.explanation: Output of gate [latex]1: \bar{C} [/latex] Output of gate [latex]2: \rightarrow(\overline{A+B}) [/latex] Output of gate [latex]3: \rightarrow(\overline{A+B}+C) [/latex] Output of gate [latex]4: \rightarrow AB[/latex] Output of gate [latex]5: \rightarrow(\overline{A+B}+C)+A B [/latex] Output of gate 6 is output Y i.e. [latex] \begin{aligned} Y &=\overline{\bar{C} \cdot(\overline{A+B}+C)+A B} \\ &=C+\overline{(\overline{A+B}+C+A B)} \end{aligned}[/latex] Using Demorgan's theorem [latex] \begin{aligned} &=C+(\overline{\overline{A+B}}) \cdot \bar{C} \cdot(\overline{A B})\\ &=C+(A+B) \cdot \bar{C} \cdot(\bar{A}+\bar{B}) \end{aligned}[/latex] Given in question C=0 [latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So, }Y&=0+(A+B) \cdot \overline{0} \cdot(\bar{A}+\bar{B}) \\ &=\bar{A} B+A \bar{B} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Output of gate [latex]1: \bar{C} [/latex]
Output of gate [latex]2: \rightarrow(\overline{A+B}) [/latex]
Output of gate [latex]3: \rightarrow(\overline{A+B}+C) [/latex]
Output of gate [latex]4: \rightarrow AB[/latex]
Output of gate [latex]5: \rightarrow(\overline{A+B}+C)+A B [/latex]
Output of gate 6 is output Y i.e.
[latex] \begin{aligned} Y &=\overline{\bar{C} \cdot(\overline{A+B}+C)+A B} \\ &=C+\overline{(\overline{A+B}+C+A B)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using Demorgan's theorem
[latex] \begin{aligned} &=C+(\overline{\overline{A+B}}) \cdot \bar{C} \cdot(\overline{A B})\\ &=C+(A+B) \cdot \bar{C} \cdot(\bar{A}+\bar{B}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given in question C=0
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So, }Y&=0+(A+B) \cdot \overline{0} \cdot(\bar{A}+\bar{B}) \\ &=\bar{A} B+A \bar{B} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: A Fourier transform pair is given by [latex](\frac{2}{3})^{n}  \; u[n+3]\overset{FT}{\leftrightarrow}\frac{Ae^{-j6\pi f}}{1-(\frac{2}{3})e^{-j2 \pi f}}[/latex] where u [n] denotes the unit step sequence. The values of A is _____.
questions.explanation:
[latex]\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} u(n+3) \stackrel{F.T.}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{Ae^{j6\pi f}}{1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) e^{-i 2 \pi f}}[/latex] Let, [latex] x[n]=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} u(n+3) [/latex] Discrete Fourier transform is given as [latex] \begin{aligned} X\left(e^{j \omega}\right)&=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{-j \omega n} \\ &=\sum_{n=-3}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} e^{-j \omega n} \\ \text { Put, } n+3 &=m \\ \text { So, } x\left(e^{i \omega}\right) &=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m-3} e^{-j \omega(m-3)} \\ &=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-3} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m} e^{-j \omega m \cdot e^{j \omega 3}} \\
&=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{3} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3} e^{-j \omega}\right)^{m} \cdot e^{j \omega 3} \\
&=\frac{3.375 \cdot e^{i 2 \pi / 3}}{1-\frac{2}{3} e^{-i 2 \pi t}} \\
&=\frac{3.375 e^{j \pi \pi f}}{1-\frac{2}{3} e^{-i 2 \pi t}} \\
\text{So,}\quad A&=3.375
\end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} u(n+3) \stackrel{F.T.}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{Ae^{j6\pi f}}{1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) e^{-i 2 \pi f}}[/latex]
Let, [latex] x[n]=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} u(n+3) [/latex]
Discrete Fourier transform is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} X\left(e^{j \omega}\right)&=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] e^{-j \omega n} \\ &=\sum_{n=-3}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n} e^{-j \omega n} \\ \text { Put, } n+3 &=m \\ \text { So, } x\left(e^{i \omega}\right) &=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m-3} e^{-j \omega(m-3)} \\ &=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-3} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m} e^{-j \omega m \cdot e^{j \omega 3}} \\ &=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{3} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3} e^{-j \omega}\right)^{m} \cdot e^{j \omega 3} \\ &=\frac{3.375 \cdot e^{i 2 \pi / 3}}{1-\frac{2}{3} e^{-i 2 \pi t}} \\ &=\frac{3.375 e^{j \pi \pi f}}{1-\frac{2}{3} e^{-i 2 \pi t}} \\ \text{So,}\quad A&=3.375 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: A real-valued signal x(t) limited to the frequency band [latex]|f|\leq \frac{W}{2}[/latex] is passed through a linear time invariant system whose frequency response is [latex]H(f)=\left\{\begin{matrix} e^{-j4\pi f}, &|f|\leq \frac{W}{2} \\ 0, & |f|> \frac{W}{2} \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] The output of the system is
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given:} \quad H(f)&=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}e^{-j 4 \pi t}, & |f| \leq \frac{\omega}{2} \\ 0, & |f|>\frac{\omega}{2}\end{array}\right. \\ \text{So, } \quad|H(t)|&=1 \\ H(f)&=e^{-j 2.2 \pi t} \\ H(\omega)&=e^{j 2 \omega} &|f| \leq \frac{\omega}{2} \\ h(t)&=\delta(t-2)\\ \text{As we know that}\\ y(t)&=x(t) * h(t)\\ \text{or}\quad y(t)&=X(\omega) \cdot H(\omega) \\ y(t)&=x(t) * \delta(t-2) \\ y(t)&=x(t-2) \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given:} \quad H(f)&=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}e^{-j 4 \pi t}, & |f| \leq \frac{\omega}{2} \\ 0, & |f|>\frac{\omega}{2}\end{array}\right. \\ \text{So, } \quad|H(t)|&=1 \\ H(f)&=e^{-j 2.2 \pi t} \\ H(\omega)&=e^{j 2 \omega} &|f| \leq \frac{\omega}{2} \\ h(t)&=\delta(t-2)\\ \text{As we know that}\\ y(t)&=x(t) * h(t)\\ \text{or}\quad y(t)&=X(\omega) \cdot H(\omega) \\ y(t)&=x(t) * \delta(t-2) \\ y(t)&=x(t-2) \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The sequence [latex]x[n]=0.5^{n}u[n][/latex], where u[n] is the unit step sequence, is convolved with itself to obtain y[n]. Then [latex]\sum_{n=-\infty }^{+\infty }y[n][/latex] is _____.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given } x[n] &=0.5^{n} u[n] \\ y[n] &=x[n] * x[n] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(k) h(n-k)\\ &=\sum_{K=-\infty}^{\infty}(0.5)^{k} u(k)(0.5)^{n-k} u(n-k) \\ &=(0.5)^{n}\left[\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} u(k) u(n-k)\right] \end{aligned}[/latex] Also we know that [latex] u[n] * u[n]=(n+1) u[n] [/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] Using the above formula, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} y[n]&=(0.5)^{n}(n+1) u[n] \\ \text{Let }p&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(0.5)^{n}(n+1) \\ \text{Also let }a&=0.5 \\ \therefore \quad p&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^{n}(n+1) \\ \rho&=a^{0}(1)+a^{1}(1+1)+a^{2}(2+1)+a^{3}(3+1)+\ldots \\ a p&=a(1)+a^{2}(2)+a^{3}(3)+\cdots \\ p-a p&=a^{0} \cdot 1+a^{1}+a^{2}+\cdots \\ p(1-a)&=\frac{1}{1-a} \\ p&=\frac{1}{(1-a)^{2}} \\ a&=0.5 \text{ or } \frac{1}{2} \\ p&=\frac{1}{\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Given } x[n] &=0.5^{n} u[n] \\ y[n] &=x[n] * x[n] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(k) h(n-k)\\ &=\sum_{K=-\infty}^{\infty}(0.5)^{k} u(k)(0.5)^{n-k} u(n-k) \\ &=(0.5)^{n}\left[\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} u(k) u(n-k)\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Also we know that [latex] u[n] * u[n]=(n+1) u[n] [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Using the above formula, we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} y[n]&=(0.5)^{n}(n+1) u[n] \\ \text{Let }p&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(0.5)^{n}(n+1) \\ \text{Also let }a&=0.5 \\ \therefore \quad p&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^{n}(n+1) \\ \rho&=a^{0}(1)+a^{1}(1+1)+a^{2}(2+1)+a^{3}(3+1)+\ldots \\ a p&=a(1)+a^{2}(2)+a^{3}(3)+\cdots \\ p-a p&=a^{0} \cdot 1+a^{1}+a^{2}+\cdots \\ p(1-a)&=\frac{1}{1-a} \\ p&=\frac{1}{(1-a)^{2}} \\ a&=0.5 \text{ or } \frac{1}{2} \\ p&=\frac{1}{\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}}=4 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The damping ratio is given as [latex]\xi=0.5[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider a communication scheme where the binary valued signal X satisfies
P{X =+1} = 0.75 and P{X =-1} = 0.25. The received signal Y = X + Z , where
Z is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean and variance [latex]\sigma ^{2}[/latex]. The received signal Y is fed to the threshold detector. The output of the threshold detector [latex]\hat{X}[/latex] is: [latex]\hat{X}=\left\{\begin{matrix} +1 & Y>\tau \\ -1&Y \leq \tau \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] To achieve a minimum probability of error [latex]P\lbrace \hat{X}\neq X \rbrace[/latex] the threshold [latex]\tau[/latex] should be

options.D:
strictly positive, zero, or strictly negative depending on the nonzero value
of  [latex]\sigma ^{2}[/latex]

questions.explanation: The optimum threshold value is [latex] \begin{aligned} \lambda_{0} &=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}\left[\ln \frac{P\left(x_{2}\right)}{P\left(x_{1}\right)}+\frac{x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}\right] \\ x_{1} &=1, \quad x_{2}=-1 \\ P\left(X_{1}\right) &=0.75, P\left(X_{2}\right)=0.25 \\ \lambda_{0} &=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\left[\ln \frac{0.25}{0.75}\right]=-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] So, [latex]\lambda_{o}[/latex] should be strictly negative.
questions.explanation_html:

So, [latex]\lambda_{o}[/latex] should be strictly negative.

questions.question:
Consider the Z-channel given in the figure. The input is 0 or 1 with equal
probability. If the output is 0, the probability that the input is also 0 equals ____
questions.explanation: [latex]\text{Given},P(X)=[0.5\;0.5][/latex] [latex] P\left[\frac{Y}{X}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} \stackrel{y_{1}}{1} & \stackrel{y_{2}}{1} \\ 0.25 & 0.75\end{array}\right] [/latex] Then [latex] \begin{aligned} P[X, Y] &=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.125 & 0.375 \end{array}\right] \\ \text{and} P\left(Y_{1}\right) &=0.625 \\ P\left(Y_{2}\right) &=0.375 \end{aligned}[/latex] and the conditional probability matrix. [latex] P\left[\frac{Y}{X}\right][/latex] is given by [latex] P\left[\frac{Y}{X}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} \stackrel{y_{1}}{1} & \stackrel{y_{2}}{1} \\ 0.25 & 0.75\end{array}\right] [/latex] Hence,  [latex]P\left[\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}\right]= P\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)=0.8[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\text{Given},P(X)=[0.5\;0.5][/latex]
[latex] P\left[\frac{Y}{X}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} \stackrel{y_{1}}{1} & \stackrel{y_{2}}{1} \\ 0.25 & 0.75\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Then
[latex] \begin{aligned} P[X, Y] &=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.125 & 0.375 \end{array}\right] \\ \text{and} P\left(Y_{1}\right) &=0.625 \\ P\left(Y_{2}\right) &=0.375 \end{aligned}[/latex]
and the conditional probability matrix.
[latex] P\left[\frac{Y}{X}\right][/latex] is given by

questions.question: An M-level PSK modulation scheme is used to transmit independent binary digits over a band-pass channel with bandwidth 100 kHZ. The bit rate is 200 kbps and the system characteristic is a raised-cosine spectrum with 100% excess bandwidth. The minimum value of M is ________.
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} B &=\frac{R_{b}}{\log _{2} M}(1+\alpha) \Rightarrow 100=\frac{200 \times 2}{\log _{2} M} \\ \log _{2} M &=4 \\ \text { So, } M &=16 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a discrete-time channel Y = X + Z , where the additive noise Z is signaldependent. In particular, given the transmitted symbol [latex]X\in \lbrace -a,+a \rbrace [/latex], at any instant, the noise sample Z is chosen independently from a Gaussian distribution with mean [latex]\beta X[/latex] and unit variance. Assume a threshold detector with zero threshold at the receiver. When [latex]\beta [/latex]= 0, the BER was found to be [latex]Q(a)=1 \times 1^{-8}[/latex]. [latex](Q(v)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi} }\int_{v}^{\infty }e^{-u^{2}/2}du[/latex], and for [latex]v\gt 1[/latex], use [latex]Q(v)\approx e^{-v^{2}/2}[/latex]) When [latex]\beta =-0.3[/latex], the BER is closet to
questions.explanation: [latex]Y=X+Z [/latex] Z is Gaussian RV with mean [latex]\beta x [/latex] [latex] \begin{array}{c} x \in\left\{-a_{1}+a\right\} \\ \text { when } \beta=0 \quad E[Y]=E[X]+E[Z] \\ E[Y]=E[X]=+a \\ B E R=Q(a)=1 \times 10^{-8} \\ Q(v)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{v}^{\infty} e^{-\frac{v^{2}}{2}} d u \cong e^{-\frac{v^{2}}{2}} \\ Q(a)=1 \times 10^{-8}=e^{-\frac{a^{2}}{2}} \\ a=6 \\ \end{array}[/latex] [latex] \text { when } \beta=-0.3 \text { mean }=6 \times-0.3=-1.8 [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} \text { So, } E[Y]&=E[X]+E[Z]=6-1.8=4.2\\ \text{So, }\quad B E R&=Q(4.2) \cong e^{\frac{-a^{2}}{2}} \\ &\cong 0.001\\ &\cong 10^{-4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]Y=X+Z [/latex]
Z is Gaussian RV with mean [latex]\beta x [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{c} x \in\left\{-a_{1}+a\right\} \\ \text { when } \beta=0 \quad E[Y]=E[X]+E[Z] \\ E[Y]=E[X]=+a \\ B E R=Q(a)=1 \times 10^{-8} \\ Q(v)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{v}^{\infty} e^{-\frac{v^{2}}{2}} d u \cong e^{-\frac{v^{2}}{2}} \\ Q(a)=1 \times 10^{-8}=e^{-\frac{a^{2}}{2}} \\ a=6 \\ \end{array}[/latex]
[latex] \text { when } \beta=-0.3 \text { mean }=6 \times-0.3=-1.8 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { So, } E[Y]&=E[X]+E[Z]=6-1.8=4.2\\ \text{So, }\quad B E R&=Q(4.2) \cong e^{\frac{-a^{2}}{2}} \\ &\cong 0.001\\ &\cong 10^{-4} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: The electric field (assumed to be one-dimensional) between two points A and B is shown. Let [latex]\psi _{A}[/latex] and [latex]\psi _{B}[/latex] be the electrostatic potentials at A and B, respectively. The value of [latex]\psi _{B}-\psi _{A}[/latex] in Volts is
questions.explanation: E is linear from A to B and E=mx+C [latex] \begin{aligned} V&=-\int_{B}^{A}(m x+c) d x \\ \text { At point } A: x&= 0, E=c=2 \times 10^{6} \vee / m =x 10^{-6}\\ \text { At point } B: x &=5 \times 10^{-6} \\ E &=4 \times 10^{6}=m \times 5 \times 10^{-6}+2 \times 10^{6} \\ m &=4 \times 10^{11}\\ -\int^{\Psi_{A}}_{\Psi_{B}} E \cdot d l&=-\int_{5\mu m}^{0}\left[20 \times 10^{5} \times 5 \times 10^{-6}+\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{2}\left[\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)-0^{2}\right]\right] \\ \Psi_{A}-\Psi_{B} &=-\left[\left(20 \times 10^{5} \times 5 \times 10^{-6}\right)+\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{2}\left[\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{2}-0^{2}\right]\right] \\ &=-\left[10+\left(2 \times 10^{11} \times 25 \times 10^{-12}\right)\right] \\ &=-15 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

E is linear from A to B and E=mx+C
[latex] \begin{aligned} V&=-\int_{B}^{A}(m x+c) d x \\ \text { At point } A: x&= 0, E=c=2 \times 10^{6} \vee / m =x 10^{-6}\\ \text { At point } B: x &=5 \times 10^{-6} \\ E &=4 \times 10^{6}=m \times 5 \times 10^{-6}+2 \times 10^{6} \\ m &=4 \times 10^{11}\\ -\int^{\Psi_{A}}_{\Psi_{B}} E \cdot d l&=-\int_{5\mu m}^{0}\left[20 \times 10^{5} \times 5 \times 10^{-6}+\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{2}\left[\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)-0^{2}\right]\right] \\ \Psi_{A}-\Psi_{B} &=-\left[\left(20 \times 10^{5} \times 5 \times 10^{-6}\right)+\frac{4 \times 10^{11}}{2}\left[\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{2}-0^{2}\right]\right] \\ &=-\left[10+\left(2 \times 10^{11} \times 25 \times 10^{-12}\right)\right] \\ &=-15 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: Given [latex]\vec{F}=z\hat{a}_{x}+x\hat{a}_{y}+y\hat{a}_{z}[/latex]. If S represents the portion of the sphere [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1[/latex] for [latex]z\geq 0[/latex], then  [latex]\int_{0}^{s}\bigtriangledown  \times \vec{F}\cdot \vec{ds}[/latex] is______.
questions.explanation: [latex]\int _s \bigtriangledown \times \vec{F}\cdot \vec{ds}=\oint _C \vec{F}\cdot \vec{dr}[/latex] (Using stoke's theorem and C is closed curve i.e.) [latex]\begin{aligned} &x^2+y^2=1, z=0 \\ &\Rightarrow \; x= \cos \theta ,y= \sin \theta \text{ and }\theta :0 \text{ to }2 \pi \\ &= \oint _C zdx+xdy+ydz\\ &= \oint _C xdy=\int_{0}^{2\pi} \cos \theta (\cos \theta d\theta )\\ &= \frac{1}{2}\left ( \theta +\frac{\sin 2\theta }{2} \right )_0^{2 \pi}=\pi\simeq 3.14 \end{aligned}[/latex]

questions.question: If [latex]\vec{E}=-9(2y^{3}-3yz^{2})\hat{x}-(6xy^{2}-3xz^{2})\hat{y}+(6xyz)\hat{z}[/latex] is the electric field in a source free region, a valid expression for the electrostatic potential is
questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{aligned} E &=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \hat{a}_{x}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \hat{a}_{y}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial Z} \hat{a}_{z} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} &=2 y^{3}-3 y z^{2} &V=2 x y^{3}-3 x y z^{2}+K_{1} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} &=6 x y^{2}-3 x z^{2} &V=2 x y^{3}-3 x y z^{2}+K_{2} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} &=-6 x y z &V=-3 x y z^{2}+K_{3} \end{aligned}[/latex] Comparing all three for uniqueness solution of potential [latex] \begin{array}{c} K_{1}=K_{2}=0, \quad K_{3}=2 x y^{3} \\ \vec{E}=-\left(2 y^{3}-3 y z^{2}\right) \hat{x}-\left(6 x y^{2}-3 x z^{2}\right) \hat{y}+(6 x y z) \hat{z} \end{array}[/latex] as we know that [latex]E=-\nabla V [/latex] [latex] E=-\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \hat{x}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \hat{y}+\frac{\partial}{\partial z} \hat{z}\right) V \quad\ldots(i)[/latex] Clearly option (D) satisfies the given relation.
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} E &=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \hat{a}_{x}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \hat{a}_{y}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial Z} \hat{a}_{z} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} &=2 y^{3}-3 y z^{2} &V=2 x y^{3}-3 x y z^{2}+K_{1} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} &=6 x y^{2}-3 x z^{2} &V=2 x y^{3}-3 x y z^{2}+K_{2} \\ \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} &=-6 x y z &V=-3 x y z^{2}+K_{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing all three for uniqueness solution of potential
[latex] \begin{array}{c} K_{1}=K_{2}=0, \quad K_{3}=2 x y^{3} \\ \vec{E}=-\left(2 y^{3}-3 y z^{2}\right) \hat{x}-\left(6 x y^{2}-3 x z^{2}\right) \hat{y}+(6 x y z) \hat{z} \end{array}[/latex]
as we know that [latex]E=-\nabla V [/latex]
[latex] E=-\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \hat{x}+\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \hat{y}+\frac{\partial}{\partial z} \hat{z}\right) V \quad\ldots(i)[/latex]
Clearly option (D) satisfies the given relation.
